title: Normal-Form Characterization of Adaptivity and Entanglement in Pauli-Based Computation
authors: Filipa C. R. Peres, Selman Ipek, Daniel Lovsted, Joshua Nevin, Anne Broadbent
abstract: Pauli-based computation (PBC) is a measurement-based model of quantum computation that samples from output distributions of universal Clifford+$T$ circuits. Here, we provide a normal form (NF) that completely characterizes its adaptive and entanglement structures. These insights unify PBC with one-way quantum computing as dual or `time-reversed' counterparts. We use the NF to advance strategies for distributed computation and investigate magic-state injection rates. We also demonstrate an exponential improvement in the detection of unnecessary magic-state qubits, allowing their efficient removal. Our NF further enables ahead-of-time circuit compilation using PBC, reducing CNOT gate count and quantum memory of random quantum circuits on average by 50% and 40%, respectively, beating other state-of-the-art compilers.
summary: This paper develops a Normal Form (NF) to mathematically characterize Pauli-Based Computation (PBC), showing its deep connection to one-way quantum computing. The key contribution is an advanced Ahead-of-Time (AOT) compilation scheme that drastically reduces resource overheads like CNOT gates and quantum memory for random quantum circuits. This work provides powerful theoretical tools for optimizing quantum circuit implementation.
main_problem: To provide a normal form (NF) that completely characterizes the adaptive and entanglement structures of Pauli-based computation (PBC).
main_result: The NF unifies PBC with one-way quantum computing (1WQC) and enables ahead-of-time (AOT) circuit compilation that significantly reduces CNOT gate count and quantum memory compared to state-of-the-art methods.
method: The authors derive a normal form by relating Pauli observables across different computational branches and constructing a bijection between PBC and 1WQC outcome records.
model_or_system: The study focuses on Pauli-based computation (PBC), a measurement-based model of quantum computation sampling from universal Clifford+T circuits. It establishes a structural duality between PBC and one-way quantum computing (1WQC).
key_observables: CNOT gate count, quantum memory size, quantum depth, and the rate of magic-state injection.
important_parameters: The number of qubits ($t$), the complexity of the random quantum circuits (RQCs), and the structure of the Clifford unitaries ($W_a$).
main_assumptions: The enhanced AOT strategy relies on finding Clifford unitaries that commute with subsequent adaptive corrections, and the analysis assumes the applicability of the Pauli measurement framework.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the PBC binary tree vs. NF tree, the distribution of Pauli measurements across processors, and performance comparisons showing AOT compilation significantly outperforms JIT compilation in reducing CNOT gates and quantum depth.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the NF to characterize PBC's structure, establishing its duality with 1WQC. It then develops enhanced AOT compilation strategies using specific Clifford unitaries to map measurements to the computational basis, culminating in performance comparisons against existing compilers.
why_interesting: While focused on computation, the rigorous mathematical characterization of resource requirements (like magic states) and the development of efficient compilation techniques are fundamental theoretical tools applicable to understanding resource constraints in any quantum physical system.

The reference branch (in black) can be determined efficiently; the NF provides a rule for obtaining any other node in the tree from the same-level node of the reference branch (orange arrows, marked with stars). (b) NF PBC tree. The NF allows us to identify measurements that belong to the same adaptive layer. (c) Fault-tolerant architecture design. The adaptive structure implies that not all magic states are needed at once (cf. Fig. 4), while the entanglement structure helps establish a suitable strategy for distributed computation. Provided there is preshared entanglement be- tween the two QPUs in the form of Bell pairs, each measure- ment in a PBC can be distributed, with the corresponding outcome obtained as m = ma ⊕mb. FIG. 5. Performance of our AOT PBC compiler for RQCs. We take the RQCs analyzed in Refs. [6, 7]. The x-axis reports the T count of the original circuits input to the compilers. The naive and enhanced AOT PBC compilers consistently outperform the JIT compiler, leading to circuits with fewer qubits (left) and CNOT gates (right). Uncertainty bars correspond to 2 standard deviations.

FIG. 4. PBC features associated with a suite of RQCs. The circuits were generated as described in Ref. [6], acting on a 7 × 7 qubit grid, with a varying T count, t = {10, . . . , 200}, and 100 circuits for each t. As t increases, so does the average adaptive depth (left). For PBCs with larger adaptive depth, the fraction of magic qubits that need to be supplied at each layer is lower (right). Uncertainty bars correspond to 2 stan- dard deviations.
